labels.reason: Historical reviewer: The rule's highest-volume false positive is "mixed together" / "mix together" (9 hits from Paul Graham essays and recipes): "mix together" is standard English where "mix" alone often does not carry the same meaning; the idiom is not redundant. Other FP patterns: (1) cooking-domain "Mix together" in recipes where it is the correct instruction term; (2) "complete stranger" as an intensifier idiom (not the same as "stranger"); (3) "while at the same time" used for medical or legal precision to stress simultaneity; (4) "brief summary" where "brief" adds useful length information; (5) "future plans" where the word distinguishes current from prospective plans; (6) "interact with each other" which is standard phrasing.
